I am a Ph.D. Candidate in the Department of Politics at the University of California, Santa Cruz, specializing in comparative politics. I am on the 2026–27 academic job market and expect to complete my Ph.D. in June 2027.

My research examines the politics of exclusion and the unmaking of citizenship in South Asia, with a particular focus on India. I ask why fully enfranchised citizens are excluded from public goods and services, and through what mechanisms this exclusion is enacted. I treat bureaucratic encounters between citizens and the state as a primary site where the substantive content of citizenship is progressively unmade and democratic erosion accumulates.

I use a multi-method approach that combines interviews, archival research, and political ethnography with computational text analysis using keyATM. My research has been supported by the American Political Science Association, the National Science Foundation (Law and Science Dissertation Grant), the Carrie Chapman Catt Prize, and the P.E.O. International Scholarship.

I hold an M.Phil. in Latin American Studies and an M.A. in International Relations and Area Studies from Jawaharlal Nehru University and a B.A. (Hons.) in History from the University of Delhi, India.

Research interests

Comparative politics, democratic backsliding, state capacity, citizenship studies, urban politics, socio-legal studies, and South Asian politics.

Fieldwork

Between 2022 and 2026, I conducted 12 months of fieldwork across six informal settlements, or “slums,” in New Delhi.

Data

Delhi Eviction Events Database

An original event dataset of more than 185 eviction and demolition episodes across Delhi, assembled from news reporting, court records, and civil society monitoring. Each entry records the date and location, the agency carrying out the eviction, whether it went ahead or was stayed by a court, the number of households and people affected, and any associated litigation, along with notes on notice periods, service cuts, and who was found eligible for rehabilitation.

Available on request.

Housing and Public Services Judgments Corpus

A corpus of more than 1,000 judgments from the Supreme Court of India and High Courts across the country, spanning 1969 to 2026, on slum evictions, rehabilitation, and residents’ access to public services. A companion corpus of more than 260 judgments focuses specifically on Delhi. Using keyATM, a keyword-assisted topic model, I trace how judges frame residents’ claims, which precedents they invoke or set aside, and how the state’s justifications for exclusion have shifted over time.
